newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close lower, fund selling seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close lower, fund selling seen.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower in moderate trade on Tuesday as portfolio-adjustment, hedge fund selling, strong economic data and heavy corporate supply took an expensive toll on prices, analysts said.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 14/32 at 96-29/32. Its yield was at 6.87 percent, up from 6.83 percent at Monday's close.
"We did have some supply pressures from some corporate bid list hitting the Street, one large one in particular," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
"I think the misperception in the bond market was that they would be selling corporates to buy Treasuries ... But I think they were selling corporates to raise cash," he added.
Money traders reported some heavy selling of corporate bonds, mainly from one large money manager which allegedly dumped some $1.5 billion in corporate issues on the market.

Analysts said part of the money raised through the corporate bond selling was said to have been channeled to futures contracts in the Chicago Board of Trade (CBT) and to the middle part of the U.S. yield curve.

"You got a lot of corporate supply dumped on the market ... Dealers tried to hedge it on the CBT and some of the flows from the corporate stuff that was sold went into the five year," said Ward McCarthy, managing director at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates Inc.
Traders also said some portfolio liquidation and hedge fund selling weighed on the market.

"You had a little bit of bottom-fishing in early trading ... but you did have some portfolio liquidations later in the day and hedge funds are continuing to sell the market as well," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Analysts said a strong 8.6 percent jump in the January single-family home sales to an annual rate of 870,000 units also poured some cold water on the market.

"We did have some strong numbers this morning. This home sales number was off the charts. We're getting a tremendous stimulus ... in the housing sector and that suggests we have upside risks to the economy," Strauss said.
The market also took in a 0.3 percent rise in the leading indicators report for January against a 0.1 pct increase in the previous month.
The market was also a bit nervous ahead of the second leg of the Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday.
Participants were glad when Greenspan said on Tuesday that his recent speeches meant to explain the Fed thinking and not to move the markets. But the bullish feeling was short-lived.

"The market tried to take a positive interpretation to what Greenspan said and went a little higher. But that was just greeted with more of the same -- selling on upticks," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A Inc.
Greenspan said during the first leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last week that he could not rule out a tightening of monetary policy as a pre-emptive strike against inflationary pressures.
The Federal Reserve added permanent reserves to the market on Tuesday through a coupon pass, but traders said the operation did little to bolster prices.

"The coupon pass was expected to happen and it didn't really move the market at all," said a trader at a foreign investment bank here. The Fed bought coupons from February 29, 2000 to February 28, 2002 for delivery on Thursday.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.10 percent. The six-month bill rate rose three points to 5.20 percent. The year bill rate was up two points at 5.40 percent.

The two-year note closed down 2/32 at 99-17/32, yielding 6.13 percent. The five-year note traded off 4/32 at 99-7/32 to yield 6.44 percent. The ten-year note closed down 7/32 at 97-15/32, yielding 6.60 percent.
